passage: Yuki had to be out of her Osaka dormitory by noon on Saturday. On Wednesday, Olga asked if she wanted help packing. "It's one room," Yuki said. "Friday afternoon, three hours, done." Friday afternoon arrived with a seminar that ran late. The boxes she'd planned to pick up from the supermarket were gone. Her books alone filled six bags, and the rice cooker wouldn't fit anywhere. At midnight the floor was still covered in clothes and cables, and the dorm office had already sent a reminder about the noon inspection. Yuki sat on her bare mattress and texted Olga, hands shaking: "Are you awake? I thought it was one room." Olga arrived at seven with tape and coffee, and they worked until the last minute.

qa.a: By noon on Saturday.

qa.q: How did Yuki feel at midnight, and what shows it?
qa.a: She was panicking; her hands were shaking as she texted Olga, 'I thought it was one room.' 😰

qa.q: What is it like for Olga to get the midnight text?

passage: In the physics department's basement lab, a paper calendar hung above Nilesh's desk with THESIS DUE circled in red on the 30th. In March he'd told his guide, Dr Bose, "I'll write it in two weeks. The experiments are done; it's just typing." Gurleen, at the next bench, had offered to swap chapter drafts early. He'd waved it off. Now it was the 24th. The references were a mess, two graphs needed redoing, and the printer on the second floor had been broken for three days. At 2 am Nilesh was still in the lab, heart racing, rewriting the methods chapter for the third time. Gurleen came in to check her samples and found him staring at the red circle. "Two weeks," he said hoarsely. "I really thought two weeks."

qa.q: Which chapter was Nilesh rewriting at 2 am?
qa.a: He was rewriting the methods chapter for the third time.

qa.q: Why did Nilesh believe the thesis was 'just typing'?
qa.a: Nilesh felt confident with the experiments done, so he pictured a smooth write-up and didn't imagine messy references, graphs to redo or a broken printer.

qa.q: What could Nilesh do even now, six days out?
qa.a: He could list what's left, ask Dr Bose which parts matter most, and take up Gurleen's offer to swap drafts.

qa.q: How might Gurleen feel finding Nilesh at 2 am?
qa.a: Gurleen may feel sympathetic, and perhaps a little sad that her early offer was waved off.

grounding: A student expects to write his thesis in two weeks, waves off early help, and panics days before the deadline.

So, Shreya, you asked why I disappeared for two weeks. I'm Manjula, and I will tell you exactly what happened.
The design internship portfolio was due on the 15th. In the first week of the month I thought, I have all my college projects, I'll just put them in a nice layout. Two evenings, maximum.

I'm Sharmila, Minakshi's roommate in the girls' hostel, and I watched the whole poster saga from my bed.
Minakshi got her research poster accepted for the state science conference a month ago. She was thrilled. "It's one A1 sheet," she said. "I'll do it the weekend before." I thought of her lab report last term, finished at 4 a.m., but I kept quiet.
The weekend before, the graphs from her data wouldn't export properly. Her guide asked for changes on Sunday. On Monday the print shop said printing would take two days. The conference was Wednesday.
Tuesday night she was pacing between our beds with her laptop, phone to her ear, begging another shop to print it by morning. I don't know everything she was feeling, but she kept saying, "It was supposed to be one sheet."
She got it printed at seven on Wednesday, still warm.

qa.q: How long did the first print shop say printing would take?
qa.a: The print shop said printing would take two days.

qa.q: What does Minakshi repeating 'It was supposed to be one sheet' suggest about how she had planned?
qa.a: It suggests she had pictured the poster as a single quick task and never imagined export problems, her guide's changes or printing time, so the delays felt like a shock.

qa.q: What could Minakshi try for her next conference deadline?
qa.a: She could list every step, including her guide's review and printing, compare it with how long her lab report really took, and start early enough to leave spare days.

qa.q: How does Sharmila see the poster rush?
qa.a: Sharmila seems unsurprised but sympathetic, having remembered the 4 a.m. lab report and watched her roommate pace between their beds.

grounding: Told by a roommate, it shows a student underestimating a conference poster and panicking near the deadline because tasks take longer than the best case.

passage: When our hostel closed for renovation, I had to move into a shared flat across town. I told Sabina it would take one afternoon. I have one suitcase, I said, and some books. What I actually had, it turned out, was two years of stuff: a mattress, a table fan, three boxes of notes, a cycle and a cupboard full of things I'd forgotten. I didn't book a tempo until the day before, and all the tempos were taken, because every student was moving. At midnight before the handover I was carrying boxes down four floors, sweating and nearly in tears. Sabina's brother drove over with his van at 1 a.m. Now, whenever I'm sure something will take an afternoon, I ask myself how long the last move took. Farhan's rule.

qa.a: Sabina's brother.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling at midnight before the handover?
qa.a: Farhan felt panicked and exhausted, sweating and nearly in tears, because the one-afternoon move had become an all-night rush.

passage:
Supervisor's note, M.Sc. thesis meetings, 2 May
In January, Amandeep told me the thesis would take "six weeks, max": two weeks of experiments, two of analysis, two of writing. I asked how long the pilot experiment had taken last year; it had taken nine weeks. He said this time he knew the methods. Today, three weeks before submission, he came to my office pale. The experiments ran until April because the incubator failed twice, and he has not started writing. His lab mate Vikas, who planned from his own pilot timings and added extra weeks, submitted his draft yesterday. I sat with Amandeep and broke the writing into chapters, with a date for each. I have also asked the department about the extension process, in case it is needed.

qa.q: How long had the pilot experiment taken last year?
qa.a: Nine weeks.

qa.q: Why did Amandeep come to the office pale?
qa.a: He felt panicked and scared, with three weeks left and no writing started, after planning only for the six-week best case.

qa.q: What did the supervisor do to help, and what could Amandeep learn?
qa.a: Broke the writing into chapters with dates and checked on an extension; Amandeep could learn to plan from past timings as Vikas did.

qa.q: How did Vikas plan differently?
qa.a: Vikas planned from his own pilot timings and added extra weeks, so he submitted his draft early.

grounding: A supervisor records a student who planned a thesis on the best-case story and panicked near the deadline.

passage: In Lunglei, Lalremsiami had three weeks left before her master's thesis was due at the college. Most of it was written, she told her friend Varun on the phone. "Just the field data from two villages. A week, maximum." Varun, who was writing his own thesis in Pune, asked how long the first village had taken. "That was the rainy season. This will be faster." But the bus to the second village ran only on alternate days. The headman was away at a wedding. Three families she needed to interview had gone to their jhum fields. By the last week she had half her data, and she couldn't sleep. She sat at her kitchen table at 2 a.m. writing an email to her guide asking for an extension, her hands cold. Varun called the next morning. "I'm asking for one too," he said.

qa.q: How often did the bus to the second village run?
qa.a: The bus ran only on alternate days.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling at 2 a.m. writing to her guide?
qa.a: She felt panicked and ashamed, sleepless with her hands cold, because the week she had planned had become three.

qa.q: What would have helped Lalremsiami plan better?
qa.a: Using how long the first village actually took, plus a buffer for buses and absent families, instead of a best-case week.

qa.q: How might Varun's call have felt to Lalremsiami?
qa.a: It probably felt comforting, since it showed she wasn't the only one who had underestimated a thesis.

passage:
The university library closed at ten, and Vidya had three weeks to submit her master's thesis. She wasn't worried. "The literature review will take two days," she told Jahnavi, her classmate. "Analysis, a week. Writing, a week."

"My thesis took six weeks," said Jahnavi. "And I started earlier."

"I work faster."

Two weeks later, Vidya was still on her literature review. Every paper led to three more. Her data had gaps. Her supervisor wanted changes to the methods.

With five days left, she sat in the library at nine-thirty, hands shaking. "I'm going to miss it."

Jahnavi sat beside her. "Everybody underestimates. Talk to your supervisor tomorrow about an extension, and let's list what's left in small pieces."

Vidya nodded, eyes stinging. She'd imagined the version where every step went perfectly. None had.

qa.q: How long did Jahnavi's thesis take?
qa.a: My thesis took six weeks.

qa.q: How was Vidya feeling with five days left?
qa.a: Vidya felt panicked, with shaking hands, sure she would miss the deadline.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi suggest, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Jahnavi suggested talking to the supervisor about an extension and breaking the remaining work into small pieces, which is realistic rather than hopeful.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi see Vidya's original plan?
qa.a: Jahnavi probably saw it as the best-case story, since Jahnavi's own thesis took twice as long.

grounding: A student underestimates a thesis, imagining every step going smoothly, and panics near the deadline.

Thank you for your advice about the scholarship application. I didn't listen, and I want to tell you what happened.

You said to start a month early. I thought, it's just forms and one essay. Two evenings, maybe three.

I started last Monday. The deadline was Friday.

The essay took three drafts. My professor needed four days to write the reference letter. The online form crashed twice. My mark sheets needed to be attested at the college office, which is only open till two.

On Thursday night I was in tears, with the reference letter still not in.

It arrived Friday at eleven, an hour before the deadline. I submitted with fifty minutes to spare.

I made it, but barely. Next time, I'll ask how long it took you, and I'll believe the answer.

Ishita

You asked why I was such a mess last June, Rekha? I'm Sarita. It was the hostel move.

The college told us to shift from the old hostel to the new block by Sunday. On Monday I thought, this will take one afternoon. I have one suitcase and a bucket.

I didn't pack until Saturday.

Then I found out I had three years of stuff. Notes, books, clothes I'd forgotten, a broken fan. The lift in the new block didn't work. The warden needed a signed form I didn't have. My roommate had already taken the only trolley.

By Saturday midnight I was crying on a pile of books.

You came and helped me carry boxes till two in the morning, remember?

I still think about it. I pictured one suitcase. I forgot the three years. Tasks always look smaller when you imagine them from far away.

qa.q: By what day did the college tell them to shift?
qa.a: By Sunday.

qa.q: How was Sarita feeling on Saturday midnight?
qa.a: Sarita was crying on a pile of books, overwhelmed because the move turned out far bigger than one afternoon.

qa.a: Rekha was probably tired but caring, glad to help a friend in a panic.

After Durga Puja, October: Binita pinned the thesis deadline, January 5, above her desk and laughed at it. "Interviews in two weeks, writing in two more. I'll be done by December." Uma, who had started in August, only said, "Transcribing takes ages."
Early December: Just six of the fifteen interviews were done. Each hour of recording took Binita four hours to type out. The fog made the morning bus late, and two farmers cancelled. She stopped going to the canteen.
January 4, near midnight: Binita sat on the hostel floor surrounded by printouts, chapter four still empty, fingers trembling over the keyboard. She called Uma, crying. "How did it take so long? I had a plan." Uma came over with her own laptop and a flask of tea, and they worked side by side until the sky outside turned grey.

qa.q: How many interviews were done by early December?
qa.a: Just six of the fifteen interviews were done.

qa.q: Why did Binita laugh at the deadline in October?

qa.a: She could have asked Uma or her supervisor how long each thesis step usually takes, broken the work into parts, and added extra time for delays.
